name: Primary Blue
lede: Primary Blue is a vivid, nearly pure screen blue, and a name that points to an old argument about which three colors can make all the rest.

sections.title: Which blue is primary?
sections.body:
Ball traces the idea of blue, red and yellow as primaries through the history of painters' and printers' colors [1][2]. Owen Jones, who decorated the Exhibition building, argued that early architecture used mostly the primaries blue, red and yellow [1]. Ball judges this largely true: Pompeii's walls blazed with vermilion, and the Greeks painted much of their stonework, which is why the old picture of plain white temples is a myth [1].

When Jacob Le Blon tried three-color printing, he needed a primary blue, and the best he had was the new Prussian blue, which Ball calls a shade too green for the job [2][3]. He also tried indigo [2]. That is the heart of the problem: no single blue works as a primary for every mixture, and no three primaries make every color, so "primary blue" names a role in a system, not one fixed color [2][3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here, #0804F9, is a saturated screen blue from the ISCC-NBS and xkcd lists, close to the pure blue of a monitor's blue light [4]. It falls in the vivid purplish blue block of the 1955 dictionary [4]. It is far more saturated than most paints, so treat it as a screen color [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering even 1% of its canvas, as photographed [5]. Closest named neighbors are [[royal-blue]], [[cobalt-blue]] and [[prussian-blue]] [4].
